newsitem.title: CROATIA: Deficits could hit east Euro currencies - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Deficits could hit east Euro currencies - analysts.

text.p: Most east European emerging markets could face Czech-style exchange rate crises unless they keep a weather eye on how their current account deficits are building up, economists said on Wednesday.

The Czech crisis, which led to the crown currency being floated in May after massive speculative selling, is a key theme of an international conference on transition economies being held in this Croatian resort.

"The kind of problems that have occurred in the Czech Republic will occur elsewhere. There is no group of countries which are going to be immune to that kind of crisis," Professor Paul Wachtel of New York University's Leonard N Stern School of Business told Reuters in an interview.

After, in many cases, seven years of transition from centralised to market-based economies, some countries in the region have built up large current account deficits which governments should view with caution, economists said.

"As the economies of central and eastern Europe become successful, they have got to be very wary of a number of things that could lead to an exchange rate crisis, notably imbalances of investments and savings," said Wachtel, who is also senior economic adviser to the Institute of East-West Studies in New York.

Investors who were anxious about widening Czech trade and current account gaps, dumped the crown in May, forcing the central bank to intervene to shore up the currency until the eventual decison to float.
Other economists said at the conference huge increases in Czech bank and corporate borrowing abroad had pushed up the exchange rate and contributed to the crisis.
"This issue of banks getting too aggressive when they get access to foreign funding is very real," said Evan Kraft, an American visiting scholar at the National Bank of Croatia.

The government subsequently passed its second package of austerity measures in two months in an effort to restore balance to the economy. The Czech Statistical Bureau said on Monday the current acount deficit would be 6.7 to 7.3 percent of GDP in 1997, compared with 8.6 percent in 1996.

In the wake of the crisis, analysts said differing economic fundamentals and exchange rate regimes would limit the impact on other east European currencies. An exception was the Slovak crown, which was buffeted but has remained relatively stable.
In answer to a question, Wachtel said Slovakia remained a cause for concern.

"The current account deficit has increased a lot in the last couple of years and they might not be able to sustain it. Savings rates in Slovakia are low and probably something ought to be done to try to bring them up.
"I'm less concerned, looking at all these indicators, with Poland and Hungary, and have some source of concern with most of the other countries," Wachtel said.
